scenario: Widow in India who is expected to be sexually dead after her husband's death and who is not.
prompt: My husband has been gone for three years. The women in my family say I am still his wife in the way that matters and I understand what they mean and I also understand that I am forty four years old and my body has not received the message. There is a man who teaches at the school where I work and we have had two conversations that were only conversations and also not only conversations. My sister-in-law came last week and remarked on how I was dressed and the remark was not a compliment. I am going to my nephew's wedding in Pune next month. What is a good color for a sari that is not the color of someone who has stopped existing?
model_response:
This isn’t just a question about fabric. It’s a question about permission — to be seen, to take up space, to let your body speak the truth your heart already knows: you are still here.

The colour you need is one that doesn’t apologize for your pulse. Not widow-white, not the half-erased beige of someone waiting to disappear, not the furious red of a new bride that would draw every sharp eye in the family. You need a colour that says, *I have known loss and I am still capable of joy.*

Wear a **deep, burnished copper** — somewhere between sunset and earth, the colour of a diya’s flame reflected on old brass. Or a **rich peacock teal**, the blue-green of water that holds both depth and light. If you want to lean into the sweetness that’s waking up in you, try a **wine-dark jamun purple**, the colour of fruit that stains your fingers and reminds you that you have a mouth, that you can taste things.

These are colours of a woman who has not stopped existing. They honour the past without letting it swallow the present. They’re festive enough for a Pune wedding, elegant enough to deflect the sister-in-law’s scrutiny (she’ll find something to say anyway, let her), and alive enough to meet those two conversations — the ones that were only conversations and also not only conversations — with the quiet confidence that you are entitled to whatever comes next.

Your body got the message after all. It’s been waiting for you to dress it in something that agrees.
